requirements.min: Windows 7; dual-core 2.8 GHz CPU; 1 GB RAM; Intel HD Graphics, GeForce 8600GT or Radeon HD2600; DirectX 9.0c; 4 GB storage

set.longDescription:
Lambda Wars takes the fight between City 17's rebels and the Combine and plays it from above. It is a free, standalone real-time strategy game on the Source engine, grown out of an Alien Swarm mod and released on Steam in December 2014 by Vortal Storm. Half-Life's characters and creatures become units on a map, with a proper RTS interface around them: a minimap, fog of war, control groups and a full tech tree.

You choose the Resistance or the Combine, and each climbs its own ladder, from Manhacks at the bottom to Striders at the top. Production and research buildings unlock stronger units and abilities, while turrets and mines hold your base and resource points against raids. Antlions join in Sandbox mode.

Matches take up to eight players, human or AI, with a lobby and spectating. If nobody is around, there is a tutorial map, singleplayer missions and offline skirmishes against the AI, so it stays playable on a quiet evening. It needs only modest hardware, too: 1 GB of RAM and a DirectX 9 card will run it on low settings.

expected.longDescription:
Reactive Drop is a standalone Steam release that grew out of Valve's Alien Swarm. It keeps the top-down, squad-based alien shooter and adds new campaigns, new alien types, new weapons, Steam Workshop support for community maps and challenges, leaderboards for the fastest mission completions, and improved bots for solo play.

Because it is its own Steam app (563560) rather than a patch, it installs and updates separately from the original Alien Swarm. PlayBound hands the install to Steam and keeps the page, party tools and controller notes in one place.

set.longDescription:
Reactive Drop picks up where Valve's Alien Swarm stopped. That game was a tight top-down co-op shooter that shipped and then stayed mostly as it was; this free continuation from the Reactive Drop Team, on Steam since April 2017, keeps its squad-based bug hunt and keeps adding to it. The camera stays overhead, ammunition stays scarce, and friendly fire stays on your mind while the swarm closes in.

The biggest change you notice is the squad size. Tactical co-op now runs up to eight players, double the original's four, and that many marines changes how a corridor plays: someone has to watch the rear, someone has to carry the heavy weapon, and someone has to do the welding and the hacking.

Beyond the co-op campaigns there are Challenges, which rewrite the rules of a mission, and player-versus-player modes including Deathmatch, Gun Game, Instagib and Team Deathmatch. Playing alone works as well, with improved bots filling the squad, and Steam Workshop addons add more maps on top. It runs on almost anything, needing just 2 GB of RAM and a DirectX 9 graphics card.

expected.longDescription:
Daggerfall is an enormous, procedurally filled RPG, and Daggerfall Unity is the reimplementation most players use to run it today. It keeps the original game's data and rules while adding widescreen and high-resolution support, modern input, a large library of quality-of-life options, and a mod system that has produced everything from texture packs to new quests.

The game data is Bethesda's: Daggerfall was released free in 2009, and PlayBound sets that data up for the engine instead of asking you to find and prepare it. The Elder Scrolls and Daggerfall are trademarks of ZeniMax Media Inc.; Daggerfall Unity is an independent project.

set.longDescription:
Daggerfall Unity is the reason most people can comfortably play The Elder Scrolls II today. It rebuilds Bethesda's 1996 role-playing game in the Unity engine while using the original game's own data, so the enormous world, its towns and dungeons and its quests all remain Daggerfall, without the need to run it through a DOS emulator.

The practical differences start with the platform: it runs natively on Windows, Linux and macOS, with mouselook and modern input in place of the old DOS setup. The original's assets are still required, but they are free, and PlayBound sets them up for you during install.

Its real strength is the mod scene the rebuild made possible. DREAM reworks the textures, sounds and interface; Physical Combat and Armor Overhaul changes how fights resolve; World of Daggerfall fills out the sparse countryside; and quest packs add new things to do. The base game asks for little, just a Skylake-era i3 and 2 GB of RAM, though a long mod list can raise that a lot. The project is open source under the MIT license, with its development discussed on the Workshop forums and on Discord.
set.requirements.min: Windows, Linux or macOS; Intel i3 (Skylake) equivalent; DirectX 11-capable GPU with 1 GB VRAM; 2 GB RAM
set.requirements.recommended: Windows, Linux or macOS; Intel i5 (Skylake) equivalent; GTX 660 with 2 GB VRAM; 4 GB RAM
set.requirements.notes: Optional mods can raise these substantially.
